profiles.name: Perry O'Brien
profiles.description: Perry O’Brien was a U.S. Army medic with the 82nd Airborne Division who served eight months in Afghanistan in 2003. After returning to the United States in June, he applied for conscientious-objector status because his military experience had led him to oppose participation in war. The Army granted him an honorable conscientious-objector discharge in November 2004. He later founded Peace-Out to assist other service members and joined Iraq Veterans Against the War and Veterans for Peace. No arrest, court-martial or confinement is documented.
profiles.finding: Penguin Random House biography confirms 82nd Airborne and conscientious discharge. Linked image is a book cover, not a portrait; asset fetch cache miss. Marquette historical journalist Perry O'Brien is a namesake.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Ralph Padula
profiles.description: Ralph Padula was a 34-year-old U.S. Army military police specialist and 11-year veteran at Fort Hood. After seeking conscientious-objector recognition and experiencing severe anxiety and suicidal thoughts, he left the post without authorization on March 27, 2003 as his unit deployed to Iraq and took sanctuary at St. John Vianney Catholic Church in Round Rock, Texas. He voluntarily returned to Fort Hood on April 9. Army officials said that his claim and possible charges remained under review; accessible reporting does not establish a prosecution, arrest or confinement.
profiles.finding: Midland Reporter Telegram return-to-Fort-Hood report and sanctuary law review match. No verified portrait in initial search.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Deshawn Reed
profiles.description: DeShawn Reed joined the U.S. Army in March 2000 and served as a human-resources specialist with the 64th Medical Detachment in Germany. Study of war and the experiences of soldiers returning from Iraq led him to oppose all military participation. He applied for conscientious-objector discharge after more than four years of service. The Army approved his application in March 2005 and honorably discharged him in April 2005. He did not serve a Middle East combat tour, and no arrest, court-martial or confinement is documented.
profiles.finding: Stars and Stripes and Sojourners match 64th Medical Detachment and 2005 discharge. Michigan criminal case is not independently matched; no portrait selected.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Tim Richard
profiles.description: Tim Richard joined the Iowa Army National Guard at age 17 in 1999. His six-year enlistment was due to end in November 2005, but stop-loss extended his obligation and his unit was called for a 608-day deployment to Iraq. Opposed specifically to the occupation of Iraq, he left Camp Shelby during predeployment training and crossed into Canada shortly before the unit’s deployment. Because his father was Canadian, Richard could pursue Canadian citizenship. The available record documents exile rather than arrest, court-martial or confinement.
profiles.finding: Captioned group-photo lead identifies back row second from left in LewRockwell article. Needs original source, clean crop and credit verification. 2017 Army Reserve mechanic and retired newspaper writer not matched.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: David Sanders
profiles.description: David Sanders was a U.S. Navy cryptologist from Arizona stationed in Florida. When he learned that his unit was being sent to Iraq, he left the base and traveled by bus to Toronto in May 2004 rather than participate in a war he opposed. He initially stayed in homeless shelters before connecting with supporters and applying for refugee status. Contemporary accounts establish his departure and political opposition but do not document a U.S. arrest, court-martial or confinement or the final military disposition.
profiles.finding: IBCC 1944 RAF portrait, historical Captain Sanders, Florida Memory and Special Forces recipient are unrelated/unverified namesakes. Movement archive remains lead.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Chris Teske
profiles.description: Chris Teske was a U.S. Army veteran of two Afghanistan tours who resisted recall from the Individual Ready Reserve for Iraq service. In a 2009 statement, he described going to Canada rather than reporting for the recall. The Nuclear Resister subsequently reported his return to the United States in 2009. The available account does not establish an individual criminal sentence or the final military disposition.
profiles.finding: wmtc January 2009 deportation report and Nuclear Resister match. No captioned portrait verified.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Harvey Tharp
profiles.description: Harvey Tharp enlisted in the U.S. Air Force in 1993 and trained as an Arabic linguist before earning a law degree and accepting a commission in the U.S. Navy Judge Advocate General’s Corps in 2000. He served in northern Iraq in 2003. After concluding that the invasion was unlawful and that further work could make him complicit, he refused another Iraq assignment and requested resignation of his commission. The Navy accepted his resignation and honorably discharged him in March 2005. No arrest, court-martial or confinement is documented.
profiles.finding: Evergreen university-hosted REPORT.pdf contains captioned Harvey J. Tharp III portrait credited Mosen Mirghanbari. Strong lead pending extraction, visual quality and rights review.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Michael Thurman
profiles.description: Michael Thurman was a U.S. Air Force intelligence specialist who opposed the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and applied for conscientious-objector status. After an eight-month application process, the Air Force granted him an honorable conscientious-objector discharge on June 10, 2008. He later became a public antiwar organizer. No arrest, court-martial or confinement is documented.
profiles.finding: In These Times 2020 report identifies Michael Thurman at front left of a 2012 protest image credited Siri Margerin. Biography confirms Air Force and 2008 conscientious objection. Group image requires clean crop verification; copyright retained, no open license established. Army veterinary sergeant and Navy staff namesakes not matched.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Wilfredo Torres
profiles.description: Wilfredo Torres was a 19-year-old U.S. Army private from Rochester, New York, who had been absent without leave for nearly a year when he publicly refused participation in a prospective invasion of Iraq. He surrendered to military police at Fort Myer, Virginia, on November 11, 2002. He was held overnight, transferred to Fort Knox the next day and received an other-than-honorable discharge the following morning.
profiles.finding: Peace-justice archive matches November 2002 refusal. 2011 Sapper photo is not independently matched to discharged Rochester private.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Marc Train
profiles.description: Marc Train was a 19-year-old U.S. Army private at Fort Stewart who went absent without leave in March 2007 rather than participate in the Iraq war. During 114 days away, he traveled to Washington, D.C., joined antiwar demonstrations and publicly explained his opposition. After returning to the Army, he received restriction and extra duty followed by a general discharge. No jail or stockade confinement is documented.
profiles.finding: Sarah Olson Antiwar.com report specifically discusses protest photographs of Marc Train. Original asset and photographer verification pending.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Jason Webb
profiles.description: Jason Webb joined the U.S. Army in 2004 and served as a telecommunications operator. While stationed in Heidelberg, Germany, he applied for conscientious-objector discharge. The Army sent him to Iraq while the application was pending, where he refused to carry an operational weapon on patrol. After an adverse recommendation, he appealed to Army headquarters. The Army approved his application and released him in April 2006. No arrest, court-martial or confinement is documented.
profiles.finding: Sojourners matches Heidelberg telecommunications operator and refusal. VMI graduate, Air Force doctor and basketball coach are not the established subject.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Travis Burnham
profiles.description: Travis Burnham was a 24-year-old U.S. Army photojournalist at Fort Drum who applied for conscientious-objector status in January 2003. USA Today reported in March that the Army was still considering the application. The accessible record establishes his request to leave military service on grounds of conscience but does not establish its final disposition or any arrest, court-martial or confinement.
profiles.finding: Movement archive matches Fort Drum photojournalist. 2021 Wyoming photographer and Reagan-era child results not independently matched; personal site needs identity verification.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Joshua Despain
profiles.description: Joshua Despain served with the U.S. Army’s 82nd Airborne Division in Iraq during 2003–2004. His experiences in Fallujah and Ramadi led him to oppose the war and the treatment of Iraqi civilians. Rather than return to Iraq, he refused further service and received a discharge in 2005. He subsequently demonstrated with Iraq Veterans Against the War. No arrest, court-martial or confinement is documented.
profiles.finding: Louisville Fellowship of Reconciliation June 2005 newsletter is a photo lead. Psychology Today counselor Joshua James Despain not independently matched.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Ghanim Khalil
profiles.description: Ghanim Khalil was born in England, became a U.S. citizen and served four years on active duty in the Marine Corps followed by four years in the National Guard. In winter 2002 he publicly announced that he would refuse deployment to an invasion of Iraq if ordered and spoke at the February 15, 2003 antiwar rally in New York. His enlistment expired before such an order, and he separated from the Guard in 2005. No arrest, court-martial or confinement is documented.
profiles.finding: NYU oral history collection and Historians Against War testimony support identity. No portrait selected; archival media follow-up remains.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Michael Sudbury
profiles.description: Michael Sudbury was a U.S. Army Reserve staff sergeant with nearly nine years of service. He requested discharge in December 2002 and publicly declared in February 2003 that he would not participate in an Iraq war. The Army honorably discharged him when his enlistment expired while his conscientious-objector request was pending. Contemporary reporting explicitly stated that he was not arrested.
profiles.finding: National Lawyers Guild On Watch Spring 2003 and Center on Conscience Reporter are leads. No captioned portrait verified.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Chris Gorman
profiles.description: Chris Gorman was a U.S. Army private first class with the 2nd Battalion, 8th Infantry Regiment, 2nd Brigade Combat Team, 4th Infantry Division. After serving in Iraq and unsuccessfully applying for conscientious-objector status, he failed to return from rest and recuperation leave in July 2006. Civilian authorities arrested him in August 2011. At a special court-martial on November 28, 2011, he pleaded guilty to desertion with intent to avoid hazardous duty and received reduction to private, six months of confinement and a bad-conduct discharge. The accessible military report does not give his arrest day or release date.
profiles.finding: Scoop interview identifies Pfc Christopher Gorman and refusal. MobyGames contributor not independently matched; no portrait selected.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Christian Kjar
profiles.description: Christian Kjar was a 20-year-old U.S. Marine from Santa Barbara stationed at Cherry Point, North Carolina. After about ten months as a military police officer, he concluded that he could not participate in the Iraq war and left for Canada in October 2005 when he learned he would deploy. He later returned to the United States to try to resolve his status, but reported severe hazing and went absent again before returning to Canada. The accessible record does not establish an arrest, court-martial, discharge or confinement.
profiles.finding: Getty caption independently matches Santa Barbara Marine in Canada since October 2005; Michael Macor/San Francisco Chronicle, rights-managed, asset 1321892459. Do not ingest licensed preview. Eyeopener article confirms identity but no inline portrait located in parsed article.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Matt Mishler
profiles.description: Matt Mishler was a U.S. Marine reservist from Florida who sought conscientious-objector discharge while facing deployment to Iraq. In a February 2008 interview summarized by The Common Ills, he described a religious objection to killing and said he would accept imprisonment rather than deploy. The record establishes his application and public position, not an imposed prison sentence or an approved discharge.
profiles.finding: Common Ills February 22 2008 identifies 24-year-old Marine reservist interview. Original movement interview remains lead; no portrait verified.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Linjamin Mull
profiles.description: Linjamin Mull joined the U.S. Army and later went to Canada rather than serve in Iraq. A Columbia Law Review study recounts his opposition to the war and his argument that military recruitment exploited economic disadvantage. Contemporary reporting said his refugee petition had been rejected by 2008. That historical rejection does not establish his eventual immigration status or any military sentence.
profiles.finding: Washington Post feature and academic study are identity-specific leads; no image attribution verified.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.

profiles.name: Derek Hess
profiles.description: Derek Hess entered the U.S. Army through the delayed-entry program in 2005. He applied for conscientious-objector status in January 2007 after concluding that participation in the Iraq war violated his beliefs. The Army rejected the application. After Hess told his superiors that deployment would make him suicidal, the Army gave him a medical discharge characterized as honorable. No arrest, court-martial or confinement is documented.
profiles.finding: Canadian Major Paeta Derek Hess-von Kruedener, Air Force colonel and Cleveland artist are distinct/unverified namesakes. Movement archive remains lead; no portrait verified.
profiles.rights: No image selected; public access does not establish public-domain status.
